# Universality for the global spectrum of random inner-product kernel matrices in the polynomial regime

**Authors:** Horng-Tzer Yau

## Abstract

We consider certain large random matrices, called random inner-product kernel matrices, which are essentially given by a nonlinear function $f$ applied entrywise to a sample-covariance matrix, $f(X^{T}X)$ , where $X\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}$ is random and normalized in such a way that $f$ typically has order-one arguments. We work in the polynomial regime, where $N\asymp d^{\ell}$ for some $\ell>0$ , not just the linear regime where $\ell=1$ . Earlier work by various authors showed that, when the columns of $X$ are either uniform on the sphere or standard Gaussian vectors, and when $\ell$ is an integer (the linear regime $\ell=1$ is particularly well-studied), the bulk eigenvalues of such matrices behave in a simple way: They are asymptotically given by the free convolution of the semicircular and Marčenko–Pastur distributions, with relative weights given by expanding $f$ in the Hermite basis. In this paper, we show that this phenomenon is universal, holding as soon as $X$ has i.i.d. entries with all finite moments. In the case of non-integer $\ell$ , the Marčenko–Pastur term disappears (its weight in the free convolution vanishes), and the spectrum is just semicircular.

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Our results

In this paper, we give a common global law for the spectra of two related families of real-symmetric random matrices which are in some sense nonlinear. Our matrices $A=A_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ and $\widetilde{A}=\widetilde{A_{N}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ , called random inner-product kernel matrices, have the entrywise form

$$ \displaystyle A_{ij} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{i},X_{j}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)&\text{if }i\neq j,\\
0&\text{if }i=j,\end{cases} \displaystyle\widetilde{A}_{ij} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{i},X_{j}}}\right\rangle}{\|X_{i}\|\|X_{j}\|}}}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{i},X_{j}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{i}\|}\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\|X_{j}\|}}}\right)&\text{if }i\neq j\text{ and }\|X_{i}\|\neq 0\neq\|X_{j}\|,\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} $$

and “give a global law” means that we find a deterministic measure $\rho$ that is the almost-sure weak limit of the empirical spectral measures

$$ \rho_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\lambda_{i}(A)},\qquad\widetilde{\rho}_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\lambda_{i}(\widetilde{A})}, $$

where $(\lambda_{i}(A))_{i=1}^{N}$ (resp., $(\lambda_{i}(\widetilde{A}))_{i=1}^{N}$ ) are the eigenvalues of $A$ (resp., of $\widetilde{A}$ ). Here $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is some fixed function, such as ReLU, representing the nonlinearity; $d$ and $N$ are parameters tending simultaneously to infinity in the so-called polynomial regime where $d^{\ell}\asymp N$ for some $\ell>0$ ; and the i.i.d. vectors $(X_{i})_{i=1}^{N}$ have i.i.d. components drawn from some fixed $\mu$ , which is a centered probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with unit variance.

Informally speaking, this normalization implies that $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{i},X_{j}}}\right\rangle/\sqrt{d}$ is order-one, and $\sqrt{d}/\|X_{i}\|\approx 1+\oo(1)$ , so that $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ are entrywise quite close. Indeed, we show that they have the same global law (i.e., $\rho_{N}$ and $\widetilde{\rho}_{N}$ tend to the same $\rho$ ). We include them both since, while $A$ may seem more natural at first, $\widetilde{A}$ has some better theoretical properties, namely it appears to have fewer outliers than $A$ (although we do not prove this in the current work, to keep this paper at a manageable length).

Our main result extends that of [LY22], which studies this model when $\mu$ is Gaussian measure, so that $A$ deals with Gaussian vectors and $\widetilde{A}$ deals with vectors which are uniform on the sphere. In the current work, we show that their result is in fact universal in $\mu$ , holding as soon as $\mu$ has all finite moments.

If the function $f$ happens to be linear, then $A$ is just a sample covariance matrix with the diagonal set to zero. (Zeroing the diagonal keeps the spectrum of $A$ from translating off to infinity; see Remark 2.6.) For general $f$ , then, the matrix $A$ is an entrywise nonlinear function of a sample covariance matrix, scaled so that the spectrum is order one, and so that the nonlinearity $f$ typically has order-one arguments. Furthermore, since $f$ is applied entrywise, any expansion $f(x)=\sum_{k}c_{k}h_{k}(x)$ induces a corresponding expansion

$$ A=\sum_{k}c_{k}A_{k}. $$

The fundamental observation of Cheng and Singer [CS13] is that one should take $(h_{k})_{k=1}^{\infty}$ to be an appropriate sequence of orthogonal polynomials, usually the Hermite polynomials. In this language, the main result of, say, [LY22] is essentially a rigorous version of the following heuristics (more precisely, the version just for integer $\ell$ ): Once placed in this basis,

- 1. the matrices $A_{k}$ in (1.3) are approximately independent;

- 2. the low-degree matrices $(A_{k})_{k=0}^{\lceil\ell\rceil-1}$ are essentially low-rank, so do not affect the global law;

- 3. if $\ell$ is an integer, the matrix $A_{\ell}$ is essentially a sample-covariance matrix, so its global law is given by the Marčenko-Pastur distribution; but if $\ell$ is not an integer then there is no matrix $A_{\ell}$ ;

- 4. each of the high-degree matrices $(A_{k})_{k=\ell_{c}}^{\infty}$ , where $\ell_{c}$ is the least integer strictly bigger than $\ell$ , has an asymptotically semicircular distribution, because they are essentially degenerate sample-covariance matrices, in the parameter limit in which the Marčenko-Pastur distribution degenerates to the semicircle law.

As a consequence, the limiting measure $\rho$ is the free (additive) convolution of the Marčenko-Pastur and semicircular distributions, with weights given by the coefficients of $f$ in its Hermite expansion, when $\ell$ is an integer; and just a semicircular distribution without a Marčenko-Pastur part, still with Hermite weights, when $\ell$ is not an integer.

In the work [LY22], the authors intially consider vectors $X_{i}$ which are uniform on the sphere, for which certain classical algebraic identities simplify the problem. Roughly speaking, the model is linearized by spherical harmonics, making it easier to see the structure of the four-step heuristic above. Then they extend from spherical to Gaussian vectors by comparison.

For general $\mu$ , these algebraic identities are not available. Instead, our proof relies essentially on a “pre-processing” step, identifying by hand which parts of $A$ (resp. $\widetilde{A}$ ) are errors, replacing $A$ (resp. $\widetilde{A}$ ) by an error-free matrix $B$ , then showing that the Stieltjes transform of $B$ approximately satisfies a self-consistent equation. The exact solution to this self-consistent equation describes the free convolution mentioned above, so we can conclude with perturbation theory.

### 1.2 Related work

An extensive history of this problem was given by the recent paper [LY22], so we only give a brief overview. Kernel matrices were first introduced in the classical scaling ( $d$ fixed and $N\to\infty$ ) by Koltchinskii and Giné [KG00]. El Karoui [EK10] studied random kernel matrices in the high-dimensional linear scaling $\ell=1$ (i.e., $d\asymp N$ ), but in a different normalization where the arguments of the nonlinearity $f$ are typically $\oo(1)$ , so that the only surviving feature of $f$ is its behavior at zero. Our scaling (where $f$ typically has order-one arguments) was first studied by Cheng and Singer [CS13], still in the linear regime $\ell=1$ , and when $\mu$ is Gaussian. As previously mentioned, Cheng and Singer introduced the idea of writing the nonlinearity $f$ in a good basis of orthogonal polynomials, which is fundamental in later works, including ours. Later, by comparing to [CS13] with the Lindeberg exchange method, Do and Vu [DV13] were able to allow for non-Gaussian data in the linear regime. More recently, Fan and Montanari [FM19] found sufficient conditions on $f$ so that, in the linear Gaussian model, the top eigenvalue sticks to the edge of the limiting distribution. As previously mentioned, two of the present authors [LY22] considered the (integer) polynomial case $\ell=1,2,3\ldots$ for Gaussian and spherical data; simultaneous and independent work by Misiakiewicz [Mis22] considered spherical or Bernoulli data for special nonlinearities $f$ . With the exception of spherical data, the previous works all focus on the unnormalized model (1.1); we are not aware of previous results on the normalized model (1.2) beyond the spherical case.

Our proof shows that the matrices $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ are well-approximated by a generalized sample covariance matrix $B$ , which we write (up to subtracting the diagonal) as $U^{\ast}TU$ . In dealing with the $B$ matrix, one technical complication is that the entries of $T$ have different scales from one another; another is that the entries of $U$ are uncorrelated but not independent; and a third is that, because of our polynomial scaling, $U\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N}$ but only with the weaker $\log M\asymp\log N$ rather than $M\asymp N$ (roughly, $M\approx d^{L}$ , where $L$ is the degree of the largest nonzero Hermite coefficient of $f$ ). Sample covariance matrices with various combinations of these technical difficulties have previously been studied in [BEK+14] and [BKYY14]. We also use several ideas from [KY17]: For example we embed our matrices of interest in a larger $2\times 2$ block matrix, inspired by [KY17, (3.2)], and ideas like their Lemma 4.6 appear here under the name of “partial Ward inequalities” in Section 5.

We also mention several related models: Instead of taking a nonlinearity of a sample covariance matrix (informally $f(X^{T}X)$ ), one can take a sample covariance of a nonlinearity (informally $f(X)^{T}f(X)$ ). This changes the limiting spectrum; for details we direct readers to works of Pennington and Worah [PW19], Benigni and Péché [BP21, BP22], and Piccolo and Schröder [PS21]. The non-Hermitian (possibly rectangular) version $A_{ij}=\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle X_{i},Y_{j}}}\right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)$ is closely related to the random-feature model (see, e.g., [RR07, LLC18, HMRT22, PW19] for this model in general, and [MM22, GLK+21, GLR+21, LGC+22, HL23] for corresponding random-matrix results, all in the linear regime $d\asymp N$ ).

### 1.3 Organization

The structure of the paper is as follows: Our main results, Theorem 2.1 (for polynomial nonlinearities $f$ ) and Theorem 2.7 (for general nonlinearities $f$ ), are given in Section 2. One main step in the proof is to replace the matrices $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ with a simpler matrix $B$ , thus separating the “main-term analysis” of the matrix $B$ , which is the bulk of the paper and constitutes Sections 3 through 8, and the “error analysis” of the matrices $A-B$ and $\widetilde{A}-B$ , which is Section 9. In Section 3 we give an overview of the main-term analysis, introducing several fundamental resolvent and resolvent-like quantities and stating that they approximately solve various self-consistent equations. In order to prove these claims, we first spend three sections establishing basic tools for our analysis: Various resolvent identities, in Section 4; variants of the Ward identity that we call “full Ward inequalities” and “partial Ward inequalities,” in Section 5; and a collection of preliminary bounds, in Section 6. We then use these tools to prove these approximate self-consistent equations in Sections 7 and 8. These sections complete the proof when the nonlinearity $f$ is a polynomial; in Appendix A we explain how to prove the general case, by approximating general nonlinearities by polynomials.

### 1.4 Notation

Stochastic domination: We will use the following notation of high-probability boundedness up to small polynomial factors, introduced in [EKYY13b]. If $X=X_{N}(u)$ and $Y=Y_{N}(u)$ are two families of real random variables, indexed by $N$ and by $u$ in some set $U$ , we write

$$ X\prec Y $$

when, for every $\varepsilon,D>0$ , there exist $C_{\varepsilon,D}$ and $N_{0}(\varepsilon,D)$ such that

$$ \sup_{u\in U}\mathbb{P}(X_{N}(u)\geqslant N^{\varepsilon}Y_{N}(u))\leqslant C_{\varepsilon,D}N^{-D}\quad\text{for all }N\geqslant N_{0}(\varepsilon,D). $$

If $X$ is complex, then $X\prec Y$ is defined as $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert X}}\right\rvert\prec Y$ . It will be convenient to write $\OO_{\prec}$ , where for example $X\leqslant Y+\OO_{\prec}(Z)$ is defined as $X-Y\prec Z$ .

We remark that our problem has two parameters tending to infinity simultaneously, namely $N$ and $d$ . The definition given here is in terms of $N$ , but one could equally write a definition in terms of $d$ (with $d^{\varepsilon}$ , $d\geqslant d_{0}$ , and so on), and it is easy to check that this definition would produce the same result. We will sometimes switch between the two for convenience.

Stieltjes transforms: If $T\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ is symmetric, we write its Stieltjes transform with the sign convention

$$ s_{T}(z)=\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{tr}((T-z\Id)^{-1}). $$

Summation conventions: We frequently consider sums over multiple indices, but include only the terms where these indices are all distinct. We indicate this with an asterisk on top of the summation notation. For example, $\sum_{a,b}^{N,\ast}f_{a,b}$ is defined as $\sum_{a,b=1:a\neq b}^{N}f_{a,b}$ ; the notation $\sum_{a,b,c}^{N,\ast}f_{a,b,c}$ means that $a,b,c$ should all be distinct (i.e., $a=b\neq c$ is also excluded from the sum), and so on. Additionally, we use standard exclusion notation like $\sum_{\nu}^{(\mu)}$ to indicate, in this case, the sum over all $\nu$ except for $\nu=\mu$ .

Floors and ceilings: If $\ell>0$ , then $\lceil\ell\rceil$ is the smallest integer at least $\ell$ as usual, but we will also need

$$ \ell_{c}\vcentcolon=\begin{cases}\ell+1&\text{if }\ell\in\mathbb{N},\\
\lceil\ell\rceil&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} $$

for the smallest integer strictly bigger than $\ell$ , and $\{\ell\}$ for the fractional part, i.e. $\{2.4\}=0.4$ and $\{2\}=0$ .

Other notation: We write $\mathbb{H}$ for the complex upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\im(z)>0\}$ , and write $\llbracket a,b\rrbracket$ for the consecutive integers $[a,b]\cap\mathbb{Z}=\{a,a+1,\ldots,b\}$ . We sometimes abuse notation by dropping “ $\Id$ ” for constant matrices; for example, if $A$ is a matrix and $z$ is a constant, then we write $A-z$ for $A-z\Id$ .

## 2 Main results

### 2.1 Polynomial nonlinearities

In this first set of results, we take the nonlinearity $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ to be a fixed polynomial (not depending on $d$ or $N$ ), expressible in the Hermite basis as

$$ f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}h_{k}(x) $$

for some $L$ and some constants $(c_{k})_{k=0}^{L}$ , where the $h_{k}$ are the normalized (non-monic) Hermite polynomials given as

$$ \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[h_{i}(Z)h_{j}(Z)]=\delta_{ij}, $$

with the first several given by

$$ h_{0}(x)=1,\quad h_{1}(x)=x,\quad h_{2}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x^{2}-1),\quad h_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(x^{3}-3x). $$

We will always work in the rectangular domain of the complex upper half plane defined by

$$ \mathbf{D}_{\tau}\vcentcolon=\{z=E+\mathrm{i}\eta:\tau\leqslant\eta\leqslant\tau^{-1},\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert E}}\right\rvert\leqslant\tau^{-1}\} $$

for arbitrary $\tau>0$ . Given $\ell>0$ , we will also need the parameter

$$ p_{\ell}=\begin{cases}1/2&\text{if }\ell\in\mathbb{N},\\
\min(\{\ell\},1-\{\ell\})/2&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} $$

where we recall that $\{\ell\}$ is the fractional part of $\ell$ . We remark that $p_{\ell}\in[0,1/4]$ , unless $\ell$ is an integer, in which case $p_{\ell}=1/2$ .

#### Theorem 2.1.

(Main theorem, polynomial nonlinearities) Suppose that $\mu$ has all moments finite. Fix $\kappa,\tau,\ell>0$ , a positive integer $L$ , and a polynomial $f$ of the form (2.1). Suppose that

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert=\begin{cases}\oo(1)&\text{if $\ell$ is not an integer,}\\
\OO(d^{-\varepsilon_{0}})&\text{for some fixed $\varepsilon_{0}>0$, if $\ell$ is an integer.}\end{cases} $$

Then, for each fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle s_{A}(z) \displaystyle\overset{d\to\infty}{\to}\mathfrak{m}(z)\quad\text{almost surely}, \displaystyle s_{\widetilde{A}}(z) \displaystyle\overset{d\to\infty}{\to}\mathfrak{m}(z)\quad\text{almost surely}, $$

with the effective bounds

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{A}(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\prec\begin{cases}\frac{1}{d^{p_{\ell}}}&\text{if $\ell$ is not an integer,}\\
\frac{1}{d^{p_{\ell}}}+\frac{1}{d^{\varepsilon_{0}}}&\text{if $\ell$ is an integer,}\end{cases} \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}}(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\prec\begin{cases}\frac{1}{d^{p_{\ell}}}&\text{if $\ell$ is not an integer,}\\
\frac{1}{d^{p_{\ell}}}+\frac{1}{d^{\varepsilon_{0}}}&\text{if $\ell$ is an integer,}\end{cases}, $$

where $\mathfrak{m}(z)$ is the unique solution in $\mathbb{H}$ to the equation

$$ \mathfrak{m}(z)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z+\frac{\gamma_{a}\mathfrak{m}(z)}{1+\gamma_{b}\mathfrak{m}(z)}+\gamma_{c}\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right)+1=0 $$

with the $f$ -dependent constants

$$ \gamma_{a}\vcentcolon=\begin{cases}c_{\ell}^{2}&\text{if }\ell\in\mathbb{N},\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\gamma_{b}\vcentcolon=\begin{cases}c_{\ell}\sqrt{\ell!\kappa}&\text{if }\ell\in\mathbb{N},\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\gamma_{c}\vcentcolon=\sum_{k=\ell_{c}}^{L}c_{k}^{2}. $$

#### Remark 2.2.

As explained in the proof of [LY22, Proposition 9], it is easy to check that (2.4) has a unique solution in the upper half plane. Indeed, as mentioned above and in the previous literature, if $\ell$ is an integer it is the Stieltjes transform of the free (additive) convolution of the semicircle law and the Marčenko-Pastur law, scaled according to $\gamma_{a}$ , $\gamma_{b}$ , and $\gamma_{c}$ ; otherwise it is the Stieltjes transform of the semicircle law, rescaled according to $\gamma_{c}$ .

The first major step of the proof is to show that, for the purposes of a global law, the matrices $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ are each well-approximated by the matrix

$$ \begin{split}B_{ij}&=\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\frac{c_{k}\sqrt{k!}}{d^{k/2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1\\
a_{1}<a_{2}<\ldots<a_{k}\end{subarray}}^{d}X_{a_{1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}X_{a_{1}j}\ldots X_{a_{k}j}\\
&=\frac{\delta_{i\neq j}}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\frac{c_{k}}{d^{k/2}\sqrt{k!}}\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}X_{a_{1}j}\ldots X_{a_{k}j},\end{split} $$

which we think of as storing the “main terms” present in $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ . (We recall that the notation $\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}=1}^{d,\ast}$ means that the $a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}$ are all distinct, but not necessarily ordered. Each of the formulations $\sum_{a_{1}<\cdots<a_{k}}^{d}$ and $\sum_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}}^{d,\ast}$ will be more convenient at some point of the proof.)

#### Remark 2.3.

We remind the reader of the usual convention that sums like $\sum_{k=\ell}^{L}$ are considered empty if, in this case, $L<\ell$ . For example, if $L<\lceil\ell\rceil+1$ , then $\gamma_{c}=0$ ; if $L<\lceil\ell\rceil$ , then $B=0$ as a matrix. In fact, if $L<\ell$ , then $\gamma_{a}=\gamma_{b}=\gamma_{c}=0$ , and Theorem 2.1 says that $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ have bulk spectra tending to a delta mass at zero.

We split the proof of Theorem 2.1 into the following two propositions. In the statements, we need the parameters

$$ \displaystyle q_{\ell} \displaystyle=\min(\ell,1,\ell_{c}-\ell)/2, \displaystyle r_{\ell} \displaystyle=(1+\ell-\lceil\ell\rceil)/2, $$

which satisfy $0\leqslant q_{\ell},r_{\ell}\leqslant 1/2$ for all $\ell>0$ . Together these imply the result, since one can easily compute

$$ p_{\ell}=\min(q_{\ell},r_{\ell}). $$

#### Proposition 2.4.

Under the assumptions above, we have $s_{B}(z)\to\mathfrak{m}(z)$ , almost surely as $d\to\infty$ , with

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{B}(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert\prec\begin{cases}\frac{1}{d^{q_{\ell}}}&\text{if $\ell$ is not an integer},\\
\frac{1}{d^{q_{\ell}}}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert&\text{if $\ell$ is an integer}.\end{cases} $$

#### Proposition 2.5.

Under the assumptions above, we have $s_{A}(z)-s_{B}(z)\to 0$ and $s_{\widetilde{A}}(z)-s_{B}(z)\to 0$ , almost surely as $d\to\infty$ , with

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{A}(z)-s_{B}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\prec\frac{1}{d^{r_{\ell}}}, \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s_{\widetilde{A}}(z)-s_{B}(z)}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\prec\frac{1}{d^{r_{\ell}}}, $$

As mentioned before, the proof of Proposition 2.4 takes up the bulk of the paper, namely Sections 3 through 8; the proof of Proposition 2.5 is much shorter, and is given in Section 9.

#### Remark 2.6.

We now explain why, in the definitions (1.1) and (1.2) of $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ , we set the diagonal entries to zero. Consider the diagonal matrices $K,\widetilde{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ given entrywise by

$$ K_{ii}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\|X_{i}\|^{2}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right),\qquad\widetilde{K}_{ii}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}f(\sqrt{d}) $$

i.e., $K$ contains the “missing diagonal” elements of $A$ (resp. $\widetilde{K}$ of $\widetilde{A}$ ), and at first glance the reader may find the matrices $A+K$ and $\widetilde{A}+\widetilde{K}$ with “restored diagonal” elements to be more natural.

Since $\widetilde{K}$ is a deterministic constant times identity, its role is easy to understand: In this case, the matrix $\widetilde{A}$ has an order-one limiting spectral measure, and $\widetilde{A}+\widetilde{K}$ simply translates this measure along the real line. According to the growth of $f$ at infinity and the power $\ell$ in $d^{\ell}\asymp N$ , this shift may be asymptotically negligible, asymptotically constant, or, in the worst case, asymptotically infinity. Proving theorems directly about $\widetilde{A}$ avoids the need to spell out these cases; the reader interested in $\widetilde{A}+\widetilde{K}$ can simply add back the shift.

Since $K$ is genuinely random, its role is more nuanced. In this case we may decompose

$$ K=\widetilde{K}+K_{\textup{fluct}}=\vcentcolon\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}f(\sqrt{d})\Id+\diag\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[f\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\|X_{i}\|^{2}}{\sqrt{d}}}}\right)-f(\sqrt{d})}}\right]}}\right)_{i=1}^{N}. $$

Of course $\widetilde{K}$ plays the same translation role as before, but the role of $K_{\textup{fluct}}$ is new: Roughly speaking, from the CLT we expect $\|X_{i}\|^{2}\approx d+Z_{i}\sqrt{d}$ , with $Z_{i}$ i.i.d. standard normal, so

$$ (K_{\textup{fluct}})_{ii}\approx\frac{f(\sqrt{d}+Z_{i})-f(\sqrt{d})}{\sqrt{N}}\approx\frac{f^{\prime}(\sqrt{d})}{\sqrt{N}}Z_{i}. $$

If $f^{\prime}(\sqrt{d})\ll\sqrt{N}$ , this suggests that $\|K_{\textup{fluct}}\|_{\textup{op}}$ is asymptotically negligible, so that $K$ is asymptotically just a simple translation as before. But if $f^{\prime}(\sqrt{d})\gg\sqrt{N}$ , then — even discarding the translation $\widetilde{K}$ — the bulk spectra of $A$ and $A+K_{\textup{fluct}}$ may be substantially different. This is potentially interesting, but to keep the current work to a manageable length, we consider only the zero-diagonal matrices $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ .

### 2.2 General nonlinearities

In these more general results, we allow nonlinearities $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ , which should still be fixed (not depending on $d$ or $N$ ), as long as they are in some sense well-approximable by polynomials. Our conditions on $f$ are the same as in [LY22, Lemma 1], and our (short) proof that Theorem 2.1 on polynomial nonlinearities lifts to Theorem 2.7 through this approximation scheme essentially mimics theirs.

#### Assumption 1.

We assume that our nonlinear function $f(x)$ is piecewise continuous with a polynomial growth rate. Precisely, there exists a positive integer $K$ , a finite subdivision $-\infty=\alpha_{0}<\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}<\cdots<\alpha_{K}<\alpha_{K+1}=\infty$ , and a finite positive constant $C$ such that

- 1. For every $i\in\{0,\ldots,K\}$ , the function $f(x)$ is continuous and bounded on the open interval $(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i+1})$ .

- 2. $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert f(x)}}\right\rvert\leqslant C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert x}}\right\rvert^{C}$ when $x<\alpha_{1}$ or $x>\alpha_{K}$ .

Under these assumptions, it is easy to show that the sequence $(c_{k})_{k=0}^{\infty}$ defined by

$$ c_{k}=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[f(Z)h_{k}(Z)] $$

exists and is square-summable:

$$ \sigma^{2}\vcentcolon=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_{k}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[f^{2}(Z)]<\infty. $$

#### Theorem 2.7.

(Main theorem, general nonlinearities) Suppose that $\mu$ has all moments finite. Fix $\kappa,\tau,\ell>0$ , and a function $f$ satisfying Assumption 1 with corresponding constants $(c_{k})_{k=0}^{\infty}$ and $\sigma^{2}$ from (2.8) and (2.9), respectively. Suppose that

$$ \frac{N}{d^{\ell}}=\kappa+\OO(d^{-1/2}). $$

Then, if $\mathfrak{m}(z)$ is the unique solution in $\mathbb{H}$ to the equation

$$ \mathfrak{m}(z)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z+\frac{\gamma_{a}\mathfrak{m}(z)}{1+\gamma_{b}\mathfrak{m}(z)}+\widehat{\gamma_{c}}\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right)+1=0 $$

with the $f$ -dependent constants

$$ \gamma_{a}\vcentcolon=\begin{cases}c_{\ell}^{2}&\text{if }\ell\in\mathbb{N},\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\gamma_{b}\vcentcolon=\begin{cases}c_{\ell}\sqrt{\ell!\kappa}&\text{if }\ell\in\mathbb{N},\\
0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\widehat{\gamma_{c}}\vcentcolon=\sum_{k=\ell_{c}}^{\infty}c_{k}^{2}, $$

then for each fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle s_{A}(z) \displaystyle\overset{d\to\infty}{\to}\mathfrak{m}(z)\quad\text{almost surely}, \displaystyle s_{\widetilde{A}}(z) \displaystyle\overset{d\to\infty}{\to}\mathfrak{m}(z)\quad\text{almost surely}. $$

We prove this result by approximating $f$ by polynomials and using the result for polynomial nonlinearities, Theorem 2.1, as a black box. This is essentially the same approach as [LY22, Theorem 2], although they can allow slightly more general nonlinearities $f$ because they have exact formulas for the distributions, which additionally have better tail decay. In Appendix A, we give the needed modifications for completeness.

## 3 Sketch proof of Proposition 2.4: Main terms as sample covariance matrices

The main idea of the proof is to rewrite $B$ in the form of a sample-covariance matrix $U^{*}TU$ , where $U$ has random, centered real entries with unit variance, and where $T$ is a real deterministic diagonal matrix storing the prefactors in (2.6). (Actually, since the diagonal terms of $B$ are set to zero, we will need to write $B=U^{\ast}TU-D$ where $D$ stores the diagonal terms.) The main technical difficulty comes from the fact that, while the columns of $U$ in such a decomposition are independent, the entries in each column are only uncorrelated, not independent. A smaller technical difficulty comes from the fact that $U$ will be of size $M\times N$ for some $M\gg N$ (roughly speaking, $M\approx N^{L/\ell}$ – and it suffices to restrict to the case $L>\ell$ , see Remark 3.1), whereas the most-studied sample covariance matrices typically have $M\asymp N$ .

To do this, we need the following notation. Fix once and for all some nonlinearity $f$ , and recall that $c_{k}$ is the $k$ th coefficient of $f$ in the Hermite basis, $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{L}c_{k}h_{k}(x)$ . For every $k\in\llbracket\lceil\ell\rceil,L\rrbracket$ define

$$ \mathbf{M}_{k}=\begin{cases}\{(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})\in[d]^{k}\text{ s.t. }a_{1}<\ldots<a_{k}\}&\text{if }c_{k}\neq 0,\\
\emptyset&\text{if }c_{k}=0,\end{cases} $$

with size $M_{k}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathbf{M}_{k}}}\right\rvert$ . We will also need their union $\mathbf{M}=\bigcup_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\mathbf{M}_{k}$ , with total size $M=\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}M_{k}$ .

For each $k$ with $M_{k}>0$ , we introduce the matrix $U^{[k]}\in\mathbb{R}^{M_{k}\times N}$ with entries

$$ U^{[k]}_{\mu i}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}X_{a_{1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k}i}, $$

where $\mu$ is the tuple

$$ \mu=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})\in\mathbf{M}_{k}. $$

Given two tuples $\mu$ and $\nu$ , we define their overlap

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle\mu,\nu}}\right\rangle\vcentcolon=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mu\cap\nu}}\right\rvert, $$

where $\mu$ and $\nu$ are viewed as subsets of $\llbracket 1,d\rrbracket$ . For example, $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle(2,4,5),(3,5)}}\right\rangle=1$ .

We also define the combined-degree $M\times N$ matrix $U$ such that $U_{\mu i}=U^{[k]}_{\mu i}$ for $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}$ and all $k$ . Note that, as claimed, $\mathbb{E}U_{\mu i}=0$ and $\mathbb{E}U_{\mu i}^{2}=\frac{1}{N}$ for all $\mu$ and $i$ ; the columns $U_{i}$ are independent for different $i$ ; but $U_{\mu i}$ and $U_{\nu i}$ are only uncorrelated for $\mu\neq\nu$ , not necessarily independent, since $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle\mu,\nu}}\right\rangle$ can be nonzero. The deterministic $M\times M$ matrix $T$ is defined blockwise

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}\ddots&&0\\
&c_{k}\sqrt{k!}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{k}}}I_{M_{k}}&\\
0&&\ddots\end{pmatrix}, $$

where we skip blocks with $c_{k}=0$ (i.e., $I_{0}$ is a $0\times 0$ matrix) by convention. The point of all these conventions is to define $T$ in an invertible way, by omitting what would otherwise be zero blocks. For example, if $f=c_{1}h_{1}+c_{2}h_{2}+c_{4}h_{4}$ and $\ell\leqslant 1$ , then

$$ T=\begin{pmatrix}c_{1}\sqrt{\frac{N}{d}}I_{M_{1}}&0&0\\
0&c_{2}\sqrt{\frac{2!N}{d^{k}}}I_{M_{2}}&0\\
0&0&c_{4}\sqrt{\frac{4!N}{d^{k}}}I_{M_{4}}\end{pmatrix}. $$

If we change this example to keep the same $f$ but let $1<\ell\leqslant 2$ , say, then the first of the three blocks disappears, and $T$ becomes smaller. Since $T$ is diagonal, we will usually write $T_{\mu}$ instead of $T_{\mu\mu}$ , and sometimes write $T_{k}$ instead of $T_{\mu}$ when $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}$ (since the value of $T_{\mu}$ depends only on this $k$ ).

#### Remark 3.1.

If $f$ has only low-degree terms, i.e. $f=\sum_{k=0}^{\lceil\ell\rceil-1}c_{k}h_{k}(x)$ , then by these conventions $T$ does not exist at all. But in this case, the matrix $B$ defined by (2.6) is zero, so $s_{B}(z)=-\frac{1}{z}=\mathfrak{m}(z)$ , where $\mathfrak{m}(z)$ is defined by (2.4), and Proposition 2.4 is immediate. For such matrices, the main result – namely, that both $A$ and $\widetilde{A}$ have bulk spectrum which is asymptotically a delta mass at zero – follows from Proposition 2.5, whose proof does not use the matrix $T$ . Thus in the following we will always assume that $f$ has some high-degree terms, so that $T$ is nontrivial.

Notice that

$$ B_{ij}=(U^{*}TU)_{ij}\delta_{i\neq j}. $$

Denote the diagonal part removed in (3.4) by $D$ , i.e. $D_{ii}=U_{i}^{*}TU_{i}$ and $D_{ij}=0$ for $i\neq j$ . The fundamental observation is that

$$ B=U^{*}TU-D. $$

Consider

$$ H(z)=\begin{pmatrix}-T^{-1}&U\\
U^{*}&-z-D\end{pmatrix}. $$

Define the resolvent

$$ G(z)=H(z)^{-1}. $$

From the definition of $H$ in (3.6) we can see that

$$ G(z)=\begin{pmatrix}G_{M}(z)&*\\
*&G_{N}(z)\end{pmatrix}, $$

where the $*$ ’s are some block matrices that are irrelevant for our purposes,

$$ G_{N}(z)=\frac{1}{U^{*}TU-z-D}=\frac{1}{B-z} $$

is the resolvent we ultimately want to understand, and

$$ G_{M}(z)=\frac{1}{U(z+D)^{-1}U^{*}-T^{-1}} $$

is an object we will understand as an intermediate step.

Throughout this paper, Greek letter indices like $\mu$ and $\nu$ will refer to the first $M$ columns and rows of $G$ , while letters like $i,j,k$ will refer to the last $N$ columns and rows of $G$ , so that for example $G_{ij}=(G_{N})_{ij}$ and $G_{\mu\nu}=(G_{M})_{\mu\nu}$ .

The fundamental quantities for the main-term analysis are

$$ \displaystyle s(z) \displaystyle\vcentcolon=s_{B}(z)=\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{tr}G_{N}(z), \displaystyle\widetilde{s}(z) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{M}\mathrm{tr}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G_{M}(z)+T}}\right), \displaystyle\phi \displaystyle=\frac{M}{N}, $$

where we have dropped $B$ from the notation $s_{B}$ to save space. We stress that $s(z)$ and $\widetilde{s}(z)$ depend on $N$ , although we suppress this from the notation. Later, we will show that $s(z)$ and $\phi\widetilde{s}(z)$ are order-one quantities for $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ . Since $z$ is fixed throughout the argument, we will often drop it from the notation, writing for example

$$ s=s(z),\qquad\widetilde{s}=\widetilde{s}(z),\qquad G_{N}=G_{N}(z),\qquad G_{M}=G_{M}(z),\qquad\ldots $$

Since $G_{N}$ is the resolvent of our matrix of interest, the eventual goal is to show that $s(z)$ approximately satisfies a self-consistent equation. To do this, we pass through the auxiliary matrix $G_{M}$ , which is not a resolvent, but which our analysis shows approximately behaves like one (for example, it approximately satisfies something like the Ward identity; see Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2). Precisely, we first show that $s(z)$ and $\phi\widetilde{s}(z)$ approximately determine each other through a joint self-consistent equation (roughly, $s(z)\approx-(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))^{-1}$ ). Then we show show that $\phi\widetilde{s}(z)$ approximately satisfies its own self-consistent equation. From here we recover the self-consistent equation approximately satisfied by $s(z)$ , which is exactly satisfied by $\mathfrak{m}(z)$ , then use perturbation theory of that equation, already developed by [LY22], to conclude. These steps are split into the following propositions, whose proofs constitute the bulk of the paper.

#### Proposition 3.2.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert 1+s(z)(z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z))}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}. $$

#### Proposition 3.3.

Let $\gamma_{a}$ , $\gamma_{b}$ , $\gamma_{c}$ be as in (2.5). For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\phi\widetilde{s}(z)-\frac{\gamma_{a}}{\gamma_{b}-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}+\frac{\gamma_{c}}{z+\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}}\right\rvert\prec\begin{cases}\frac{1}{d^{q_{\ell}}}&\text{if $\ell$ is not an integer,}\\
\frac{1}{d^{q_{\ell}}}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert&\text{if $\ell$ is an integer.}\end{cases} $$

#### Proposition 3.4.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{1}{s(z)}+z+\frac{\gamma_{a}s(z)}{1+\gamma_{b}s(z)}+\gamma_{c}s(z)}}\right\rvert\prec\begin{cases}\frac{1}{d^{q_{\ell}}}&\text{if $\ell$ is not an integer,}\\
\frac{1}{d^{q_{\ell}}}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert&\text{if $\ell$ is an integer.}\end{cases} $$

Modulo Propositions 3.2, 3.3, and 3.4, the proof of Proposition 2.4 is quite short. We re-write (2.4), $1+\mathfrak{m}(z)(z+\gamma_{a}\mathfrak{m}(z)/(1+\gamma_{b}\mathfrak{m}(z))+\gamma_{c}\mathfrak{m}(z))=0$ , as

$$ \frac{1}{\mathfrak{m}(z)}+z+\frac{\gamma_{a}\mathfrak{m}(z)}{1+\gamma_{b}\mathfrak{m}(z)}+\gamma_{c}\mathfrak{m}(z)=0, $$

in order to recall the following stability analysis of this equation, due to [LY22].

#### Lemma 3.5.

[LY22, Proposition 9] If deterministic $\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{s}(z)$ approximately solves (3.13) in the sense that

$$ \frac{1}{\mathfrak{s}}+z+\frac{\gamma_{a}\mathfrak{s}}{1+\gamma_{b}\mathfrak{s}}+\gamma_{c}\mathfrak{s}=\omega $$

with the error term $\omega$ satisfying

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\omega}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{\eta}{2},\quad\eta=\im(z), $$

and $\mathfrak{m}=\mathfrak{m}(z)$ exactly solves (3.13), then

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathfrak{s}-\mathfrak{m}}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{4\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\omega}}\right\rvert}{\eta^{2}}. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 2.4.

Write

$$ \omega\vcentcolon=\frac{1}{s(z)}+z+\frac{\gamma_{a}s(z)}{1+\gamma_{b}s(z)}+\gamma_{c}s(z). $$

Let $\delta_{\ell}=q_{\ell}$ , if $\ell$ is not an integer, or $\delta_{\ell}=\min(q_{\ell},\varepsilon_{0})$ , if $\ell$ is an integer. For $\varepsilon<\delta_{\ell}$ , applying Lemma 3.5, we find

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert\geqslant d^{\varepsilon-\delta_{\ell}}) \displaystyle\leqslant\mathbb{P}(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\omega}}\right\rvert\geqslant\eta/2)+\mathbb{P}(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert\geqslant d^{\varepsilon-\delta_{\ell}},\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\omega}}\right\rvert\leqslant\eta/2) \displaystyle\leqslant\mathbb{P}(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\omega}}\right\rvert\geqslant\eta/2)+\mathbb{P}(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\omega}}\right\rvert\geqslant(\eta^{2}/4)d^{\varepsilon-\delta_{\ell}}) \displaystyle\leqslant 2\mathbb{P}(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\omega}}\right\rvert\geqslant(\eta^{2}/4)d^{\varepsilon-\delta_{\ell}}) \displaystyle\leqslant C_{\varepsilon,D}d^{-D}, $$

where the last inequality follows from Proposition 3.4 for $d$ sufficiently large. This verifies (2.7), and the almost-sure convergence of $s(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)$ to zero follows from the Borel-Cantelli lemma. (This is why we require $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert\leqslant d^{-\varepsilon_{0}}$ when $\ell$ is an integer; if e.g. $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\frac{N}{d^{\ell}}-\kappa}}\right\rvert\sim\frac{1}{\log(d)}$ , then this argument would give $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)-\mathfrak{m}(z)}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{d^{\varepsilon}}{\log(d)}$ for all $d$ sufficiently large, which is of course insufficient for almost-sure convergence.) ∎

## 4 Basic tools: Resolvent identities

The goal of this section is to prove several exact equalities relating $G_{N}$ , $G_{M}$ , and their corresponding minors, which will be used throughout the paper.

#### Definition 4.1 (Minors).

The matrix $H(z)$ from (3.6) is $(M+N)\times(M+N)$ . If $E\subset\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket$ is any so-called exclusion set, we will write $H^{(E)}(z)$ for the $(M+(N-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert E}}\right\rvert))\times(M+(N-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert E}}\right\rvert))$ matrix obtained from $H(z)$ given by erasing the rows and columns indicated by $E$ . Most frequently we will use $E=\{i\}$ for some index $i$ , in which case we abuse notation by writing $H^{(i)}$ instead of $H^{(\{i\})}$ . We define the corresponding resolvent by

$$ G^{(E)}(z)\vcentcolon=H^{(E)}(z)^{-1}. $$

If $E=\emptyset$ , by convention we set $H^{(E)}=H$ and $G^{(E)}=G$ . Although $H^{(E)}(z)$ and $G^{(E)}(z)$ have fewer rows and columns than $H(z)$ and $G(z)$ , we keep the original values of the matrix indices: For example, $G^{(i)}(z)$ has entries $G^{(i)}_{jk}$ for $j,k\in\{1,\ldots,i-1,i+1,\ldots,N\}$ , not $\{1,\ldots,N-1\}$ .

Notice from the definition that we will only ever need minors that remove some $i$ and $j$ indices, never those that remove some $\mu$ and $\nu$ indices.

Recall that $G_{N}=(B-z)^{-1}$ , where $B_{ij}=U_{i}^{\ast}TU_{j}\delta_{i\neq j}$ . We introduce the notation $B_{j}$ for the $j$ -th column of $B$ with diagonal element excluded, i.e. $B_{j}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{1j},\ldots,B_{j-1,j},B_{j+1,j},\ldots,B_{Nj}}}\right)^{T}$ .

#### Lemma 4.2 (Resolvent identities).

For any $i$ , any $\mu$ , and any (possibly empty) exclusion set $E$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle G_{\mu\nu}^{(i)} \displaystyle=G_{\mu\nu}-\frac{G_{\mu i}G_{i\nu}}{G_{ii}} \displaystyle G_{i\mu} \displaystyle=-G_{ii}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbf{M}}U_{\alpha i}G_{\alpha\mu}^{(i)} \displaystyle G_{ii} \displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-z-\sum_{\mu,\nu\in\mathbf{M}}U_{\mu i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G^{(i)}_{M}+T}}\right)_{\mu\nu}U_{\nu i}}}\right)^{-1}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-z-D_{ii}-\sum_{\mu,\nu\in\mathbf{M}}U_{\mu i}G^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}U_{\nu i}}}\right)^{-1} \displaystyle G_{M}^{(E)}+T \displaystyle=TU^{(E)}G_{N}^{(E)}(U^{(E)})^{\ast}T \displaystyle(G_{M}+T)_{\mu\nu} \displaystyle=-T_{\mu}\sum_{j=1}^{N}G_{jj}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbf{M}}U_{\mu j}U_{\alpha j}G_{\alpha\nu}^{(j)} $$

#### Proof.

The identities (4.1) and (4.2) are very standard in the local-law literature (see, e.g., [BGK16, Lemma 3.5] for a proof). The usual version of (4.2) simplifies to what we have written here since the $N\times N$ block of $H$ is diagonal, i.e. $H_{ik}=0$ for $i\neq k$ , so that

$$ G_{i\mu}=-G_{ii}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbf{M}}U_{\alpha i}G_{\alpha\mu}^{(i)}+\sum_{k}^{(i)}H_{ik}G_{k\mu}^{(i)}}}\right)=-G_{ii}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbf{M}}U_{\alpha i}G_{\alpha\mu}^{(i)}. $$

The identity (4.3) is just the usual Schur complement formula, again summing only over $\mu$ and $\nu$ for the same reason.

In proving (4.4), by erasing rows and columns as necessary we may assume $E=\emptyset$ ; then it is a simple arithmetic consequence of the formulas (3.9) and (3.10) for $G_{N}$ and $G_{M}$ , respectively. Namely, (3.9) gives

$$ \Id=G_{N}(U^{\ast}TU-D-z)=G_{N}U^{\ast}TU-G_{N}(z+D), $$

so

$$ (z+D)^{-1}-G_{N}U^{\ast}TU(z+D)^{-1}+G_{N}=(\Id-G_{N}U^{\ast}TU)(z+D)^{-1}+G_{N}=-G_{N}(z+D)(z+D)^{-1}+G_{N}=0, $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\Id \displaystyle=\Id-TU[(z+D)^{-1}-G_{N}U^{\ast}TU(z+D)^{-1}+G_{N}]U^{\ast} \displaystyle=-TU(z+D)^{-1}U^{\ast}+\Id+TUG_{N}U^{\ast}TU(z+D)^{-1}U^{\ast}-TUG_{N}U^{\ast}TT^{-1} \displaystyle=(-T+TUG_{N}U^{\ast}T)(U(z+D)^{-1}U^{\ast}-T^{-1}) \displaystyle=(-T+TUG_{N}U^{\ast}T)G_{M}^{-1}, $$

where the last equality is (3.10). This means that

$$ G_{M}=-T+TUG_{N}U^{\ast}T, $$

which can be rearranged to obtain (4.4).

The proof of (4.5) is the most involved. It starts with the Sherman–Morrison formula for the inverse of a rank-one update, which is usually formulated for a matrix $A$ , column vector $q$ , and scalar $\tau$ as

$$ (A+\tau qq^{\ast})^{-1}=A^{-1}-\frac{\tau A^{-1}qq^{\ast}A^{-1}}{1+\tau q^{\ast}A^{-1}q}. $$

Left-multiplying by $q^{\ast}$ and simplifying on the right-hand side, we obtain

$$ q^{\ast}(A+\tau qq^{\ast})^{-1}=\frac{(1+\tau q^{\ast}A^{-1}q)q^{\ast}A^{-1}-\tau q^{\ast}A^{-1}qq^{\ast}A^{-1}}{1+\tau q^{\ast}A^{-1}q}=\frac{1}{1+\tau q^{\ast}A^{-1}q}q^{\ast}A^{-1}. $$

If we use this with $q=U_{j}$ , $\tau=(z+D_{j})^{-1}$ , and $A=U(z+D)^{-1}U^{\ast}-U_{j}(z+D_{j})^{-1}U_{j}^{\ast}-T^{-1}=(G_{M}^{(j)})^{-1}$ , so that $A+\tau qq^{\ast}=(G_{M})^{-1}$ , we obtain an equation over vectors of length $M$ ; taking the $\nu$ entry of each side, we find

$$ \sum_{\alpha}U_{\alpha j}G_{\alpha\nu}=\frac{1}{1+(z+D_{j})^{-1}U_{j}^{\ast}G_{M}^{(j)}U_{j}}\sum_{\alpha}U_{\alpha j}G^{(j)}_{\alpha\nu}. $$

Store this for a moment; at the same time, rearrange (3.10) to obtain

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U(z+D)^{-1}U^{*}-T^{-1}}}\right)G_{M}=\Id, $$

then take the $(\mu\nu)$ entry of both sides to get

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{j}(z+D_{j})^{-1}}}\right)U_{\mu j}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{\alpha}U_{\alpha j}G_{\alpha\nu}}}\right)-T_{\mu}^{-1}G_{\mu\nu}=\delta_{\mu\nu}. $$

Now we substitute (4.6) into the left-hand side, and multiply both sides by $T_{\mu}$ ; this yields

$$ \sum_{j}\frac{T_{\mu}}{z+D_{j}+U_{j}^{\ast}G_{M}^{(j)}U_{j}}\sum_{\alpha}U_{\mu j}U_{\alpha j}G^{(j)}_{\alpha\nu}-G_{\mu\nu}=T_{\mu\nu}. $$

Substituting $\frac{1}{z+D_{j}+U_{j}^{\ast}G_{M}^{(j)}U_{j}}=-G_{jj}$ , from (4.3), finishes the proof of (4.5). ∎

## 5 Basic tools: Full and partial Ward inequalities

Since $G_{N}=(B-z)^{-1}$ is actually a resolvent, it satisfies the usual Ward identity

$$ G_{N}G_{N}^{*}=\frac{\im G_{N}}{\eta}, $$

where $\eta=\im z$ , and actually the extension to minors

$$ G_{N}^{(E)}(G_{N}^{(E)})^{\ast}=\frac{\im G_{N}^{(E)}}{\eta}. $$

Since $G_{M}+T$ is not a resolvent, it does not satisfy the Ward identity. However, the goal of this section is to show that it approximately satisfies an inequality that looks like one direction of the Ward identity (roughly speaking, $(G_{M}+T)(G_{M}+T)^{\ast}\lesssim\im(G_{M}+T)/\eta$ , or in coordinates $\sum_{\nu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}+T)_{\mu\nu}}}\right\rvert^{2}\lesssim\im(G_{M}+T)_{\mu\mu}/\eta$ ; then $\im(T)$ disappears since $T$ is real). This says that, for each $\mu$ , the sum of $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}+T)_{\mu\nu}}}\right\rvert^{2}$ over $\nu$ is much smaller than a naive estimate would predict. Actually we show something better, which is crucial for our proof of Lemma 3.2: This sum is also smaller than expected if it is taken, not over all tuples $\nu$ , but just over some of them, namely those with a fixed overlap with $\mu$ . (Recall that $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle\mu,\nu}}\right\rangle$ denotes the overlap of the multi-indices $\mu$ and $\nu$ , i.e., the number of $X$ ’s they have in common.) We call such estimates partial Ward inequalities, in contrast with the original estimates, which we call full Ward inequalities.

#### Lemma 5.1 (Full Ward inequality).

For any $\mu$ , and any (possibly empty) exclusion set $E\subset[N]$ with size $\OO(1)$ , we have

$$ \sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G^{(E)}_{M}+T)_{\mu\nu}}}\right\rvert^{2}\prec\frac{\im G^{(E)}_{\mu\mu}}{\eta}, $$

uniformly over $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}$ .

Note that full Ward inequality follows directly from partial Ward inequalities, so we omit the proof.

#### Lemma 5.2 (Partial Ward inequality).

For any $k_{1},k_{2}\in\llbracket\lceil\ell\rceil,L\rrbracket$ , $t\in\llbracket 0,\min(k_{1},k_{2})\rrbracket$ and $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k_{1}}$ , let

$$ S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\nu\in\mathbf{M}_{k_{2}}\mid\langle\mu,\nu\rangle=t}}\right\}. $$

Then for any $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k_{1}}$ and any (possibly empty) exclusion set $E\subset[N]$ with size $\OO(1)$ , we have

$$ \sum_{\nu\in S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|(G_{M}^{(E)}+T)_{\mu\nu}}}\right|^{2}\prec\frac{\im G^{(E)}_{\mu\mu}}{\eta}d^{\max\{-t,\ell-k_{2}\}}, $$

uniformly over $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k_{1}}$ .

#### Proof of Lemma 5.2.

For notational simplicity, let $S\vcentcolon=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}\right\rvert$ and $\tilde{N}\vcentcolon=N-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert E}}\right\rvert$ . Because of our convention that $\mathbf{M}_{k}=\emptyset$ when the $k$ th Hermite coefficient of $f$ vanishes, we can have $S=0$ , but in this case (5.3) is trivial, so we can and will assume $S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}\neq\emptyset$ . Consider the restrictions of $T$ and $U$ to this subset, denoted by $T\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}$ and $U\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}$ ; these are matrices of size $S\times S$ and $S\times\tilde{N}$ , respectively, and $T\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}=c_{k_{2}}\sqrt{\frac{k_{2}!N}{d^{k_{2}}}}I$ . We will write $(U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}})_{i}$ for the $i$ th column of $U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}$ . Using the resolvent identity $G_{M}^{(E)}+T=TU^{(E)}G_{N}^{(E)}(U^{(E)})^{\ast}T$ from (4.4), we can view the left-hand side of (5.3) as

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\nu\in S^{k_{2},t}_{\mu}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|(G_{M}^{(E)}+T)_{\mu\nu}}}\right|^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{\nu\in S^{k_{2},t}_{\mu}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(TU^{(E)}G_{N}^{(E)}(U^{(E)})^{\ast}T)_{\mu\nu}}}\right\rvert^{2}=\sum_{\nu\in S^{k_{2},t}_{\mu}}\sum_{i,j,k,\ell=1}^{N,(E)}T_{\mu}U_{\mu i}G_{ij}U_{\nu j}T_{\nu}T_{\nu}U_{\nu k}(G^{\ast})_{k\ell}U_{\mu\ell}T_{\mu} \displaystyle=c_{k_{2}}^{2}k_{2}!\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\sum_{\nu\in S^{k_{2},t}_{\mu}}\sum_{i,j,k,\ell=1}^{N,(E)}T_{\mu}U_{\mu i}G_{ij}U_{\nu j}U_{\nu k}(G^{\ast})_{k\ell}U_{\mu\ell}T_{\mu} \displaystyle=c_{k_{2}}^{2}k_{2}!\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\sum_{i,j,k,\ell=1}^{N,(E)}T_{\mu}U_{\mu i}G_{ij}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}^{*}U\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right)_{jk}(G^{\ast})_{k\ell}(U^{\ast})_{\ell\mu}T_{\mu} \displaystyle=c_{k_{2}}^{2}k_{2}!\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(T_{\mu}U^{(E)}G_{N}^{(E)}U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}^{*}U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}(G_{N}^{(E)})^{*}(U^{(E)})^{*}T_{\mu}}}\right)_{\mu\mu} \displaystyle=c_{k_{2}}^{2}k_{2}!\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle((G_{N}^{(E)})^{\ast}(U^{(E)})^{\ast}Te_{\mu}),\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}^{*}U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right)((G_{N}^{(E)})^{\ast}(U^{(E)})^{\ast}Te_{\mu})}}\right\rangle $$

(recalling that notations like $\sum_{i=1}^{N,(E)}$ mean summing over indices $i\in\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket\setminus E$ ), where $e_{\mu}$ is the standard basis vector of size $S\times 1$ , so that $(G_{N}^{(E)})^{\ast}(U^{(E)})^{\ast}Te_{\mu}$ is a vector in $\mathbb{C}^{\tilde{N}}$ . Bounding the quadratic form by the operator norm times the vector norm, then applying the (non-partial) Ward identity (5.2) for $G_{N}$ , we find

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\nu\in S^{t}_{\mu}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|(G_{M}^{(E)}+T)_{\mu\nu}}}\right|^{2} \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}^{*}U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(TU^{(E)}G_{N}^{(E)}(G_{N}^{(E)})^{*}(U^{(E)})^{*}T}}\right)_{\mu\mu} \displaystyle=\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}^{*}U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}\frac{1}{\eta}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(TU^{(E)}\im G_{N}^{(E)}(U^{(E)})^{*}T}}\right)_{\mu\mu} \displaystyle=\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}^{*}U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}\frac{\im G^{(E)}_{\mu\mu}}{\eta}, $$

where in the last equality we use that $T$ and $U^{(E)}$ have real entries, so that

$$ TU^{(E)}\im G_{N}^{(E)}(U^{(E)})^{\ast}T=\im(TU^{(E)}G_{N}^{(E)}(U^{(E)})^{\ast}T), $$

and once again the identity $G_{M}^{(E)}+T=TU^{(E)}G_{N}^{(E)}(U^{(E)})^{\ast}T$ from (4.4).

It remains to show that

$$ \frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}^{*}U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}\prec d^{\max\{-t,\ell-k_{2}\}}=\vcentcolon\Phi. $$

Since the distribution of the left-hand side depends only on the length of $\mu$ and not which $X$ ’s it contains, the final result (5.3) will be uniform in $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k_{1}}$ as claimed.

Recall that the columns $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right)_{i}$ are independent; thus, since $\|AA^{\ast}\|_{\textup{op}}=\|A^{\ast}A\|_{\textup{op}}$ ,

$$ \begin{split}\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}^{*}U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}&=\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}U^{(E)}\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}^{*}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}\\
&=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N,(E)}\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right)_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right)_{i}^{*}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}=\vcentcolon\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N,(E)}Z_{i}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}\end{split} $$

reduces the problem to bounding the operator norm a sum of independent and identically distributed matrices $Z=\sum_{i=1}^{N,(E)}Z_{i}$ , each $Z_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times S}$ , which we can do with the matrix Bernstein inequality (see, e.g., Theorem 5.4.1 of [Ver18]). Notice that matrices $Z_{i}$ are not centered and do not have bounded norm; thus we need to modify them to use this inequality. To simplify the notation, from now on, we assume without loss of generality that $E=\llbracket N-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert E}}\right\rvert+1,\ldots,N\rrbracket$ , so that $\sum_{i=1}^{N,(E)}=\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{N}}$ . We additionally abuse notation by writing $N$ instead of $\tilde{N}$ ; this is fine in asymptotics since $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert E}}\right\rvert=\OO(1)$ .

To show (5.12), it suffices to show that for any $\varepsilon,D>0$ there is $N_{0}(\varepsilon,D)\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ such that for any $N\geqslant N_{0}(\varepsilon,D)$ the following inequality holds:

$$ \mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}>d^{\varepsilon}\Phi}}\right)\leqslant N^{-D}. $$

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and $D>0$ . Pick $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon/2)$ . Define the centered matrices

$$ \tilde{Z}_{i}=Z_{i}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})-\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[Z_{i}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})}}\right]. $$

Notice that

$$ \|Z_{i}\|=\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U\big|_{S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}}\right)_{i}}}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\sum_{\alpha\in S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}U_{\alpha i}^{2}\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|S_{\mu}^{k_{2},t}}}\right|\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\frac{1}{N}\prec d^{k_{2}-t}d^{-k_{2}}=d^{-t}, $$

and this bound is uniform in $i\in[N]$ , as the $Z_{i}$ are independent and identically distributed matrices. Then there exists $\tilde{N}_{0}$ such that for any $N\geqslant\tilde{N}_{0}$ we have

$$ \mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\|Z_{i}\|>d^{-t+\delta}}}\right)\leqslant N^{-D-2} $$

for all $i\in[N]$ . Consider the event

$$ \Omega(N,\varepsilon,D)=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\forall i\in[N]\vcentcolon\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta}}}\right\}. $$

We will use it later to upgrade the result of matrix Bernstein inequality from $\tilde{Z}_{i}$ to $Z_{i}$ ; for now we just store that, from (5.17) and the union bound, we have

$$ \mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\Omega(N,\varepsilon,D)}}\right)\geqslant 1-N^{-D-1}. $$

The matrix Bernstein inequality for the real-symmetric $S\times S$ matrices $(\tilde{Z}_{i})_{i=1}^{N}$ reads

$$ \mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{Z}_{i}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}>t}}\right)\leqslant 2S\exp\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-\frac{t^{2}/2}{\sigma^{2}+Kt/3}}}\right) $$

for any $t>0$ , where $\max_{i}\|\tilde{Z}_{i}\|_{\textup{op}}\leqslant K$ almost surely and $\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}_{i}^{2}]\|_{\textup{op}}\leqslant\sigma^{2}$ . Thus we need to give deterministic upper bounds for $\|\tilde{Z}_{i}\|$ and $\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}_{i}^{2}]\|$ . First, we bound their norm as

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\tilde{Z}_{i}}}\right\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[Z_{i}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})}}\right]}}\right\|, $$

and since $Z_{i}$ is positive semidefinite we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[Z_{i}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})}}\right]}}\right\|=\max_{\lVert v\rVert=1}\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[v^{\ast}Z_{i}v\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})}}\right]\leqslant\max_{\lVert v\rVert=1}\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[v^{\ast}Z_{i}v}}\right]=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\mathbb{E}Z_{i}}}\right\|. $$

Notice that $Z_{i}$ has the form $Z_{i}=\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}vv^{\ast}$ for a vector $v\in\mathbb{R}^{S}$ with uncorrelated coordinates $v_{\nu}=U_{\nu i}$ ; thus $\mathbb{E}Z_{i}=\frac{1}{N}\cdot\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}\Id=\frac{1}{d^{k_{2}}}\Id$ . In the following we allow $C$ to change from line to line. Since $t\leqslant k_{2}$ and $\delta$ is small, we thus have

$$ \|\widetilde{Z}_{i}\|\leqslant Cd^{-t+\delta}. $$

Next, we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}_{i}^{2}]\| \displaystyle=\|\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{2}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})]-(\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})])^{2}\| \displaystyle\leqslant\|\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{2}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})]\|+\|\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})])\|^{2}. $$

The second term on the right-hand side has been studied above. We only need to provide an estimate for the first term. Since $Z_{i}=\frac{N}{d^{k_{2}}}vv^{\ast}$ , we also have $Z_{i}^{2}=Z_{i}\|Z_{i}\|$ ; using this identity, we find

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}^{2}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})]\| \displaystyle=\max_{\lVert v\rVert=1}\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[v^{\ast}Z_{i}v\|Z_{i}\|\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})}}\right]\leqslant d^{-t+\delta}\max_{\lVert v\rVert=1}\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[v^{\ast}Z_{i}v}}\right] \displaystyle=d^{-t+\delta}\|\mathbb{E}Z_{i}\|\leqslant Cd^{-t-k_{2}+\delta}. $$

Since the $\tilde{Z}_{i}$ are i.i.d. over $i$ , we thus have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}_{i}^{2}]}}\right\|=N\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}_{i}^{2}]}}\right\|\leqslant Cd^{\delta}(Nd^{-t-k_{2}}+Nd^{-2k_{2}})\leqslant Cd^{\delta}d^{\ell-t-k_{2}}\leqslant Cd^{\delta}d^{2\max(-t,\ell-k_{2})}\leqslant Cd^{\delta}\Phi^{2}, $$

since $t<k_{2}$ and since $a+b\leqslant 2\max(a,b)$ for real $a,b$ .

Now we can plug these estimates into the matrix Bernstein inequality (5.20), choosing $t=d^{\varepsilon/2}\Phi$ , $K=Cd^{-t+\delta}$ , and $\sigma^{2}=Cd^{\delta}\Phi^{2}$ to obtain

$$ \mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{Z}_{i}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}>d^{\varepsilon/2}\Phi}}\right)\leqslant 2S\exp\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-\frac{d^{\varepsilon}\Phi^{2}/2}{Cd^{\delta}\Phi^{2}+Cd^{-t+\delta}d^{\varepsilon/2}\Phi}}}\right). $$

Since $\Phi=d^{\max\{-t,\ell-k_{2}\}}$ , we have $Cd^{\delta}\Phi^{2}+Cd^{-t+\delta}d^{\varepsilon/2}\Phi\leqslant C\Phi^{2}d^{\delta+\varepsilon/2}$ . Thus the argument of the exponential is upper-bounded by $-Cd^{\varepsilon/2-\delta}$ ; since $S$ grows polynomially in $d$ and $\delta<\varepsilon/2$ , this implies

$$ \mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{Z}_{i}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}>d^{\varepsilon/2}\Phi}}\right)\leqslant N^{-D-1} $$

for sufficiently large $N$ .

To upgrade this to an estimate on $\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}\|_{\textup{op}}$ , we introduce the event

$$ \tilde{\Omega}(N,\varepsilon,D)=\Omega(N,\varepsilon,D)\cap\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{Z}_{i}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}\leqslant d^{\varepsilon/2}\Phi}}\right\}. $$

Combining (5.21) with (5.19) gives us

$$ \mathbb{P}(\tilde{\Omega}(N,\varepsilon,D)^{c})\leqslant N^{-D} $$

for large enough $N$ . Furthermore, on this event, we have $\tilde{Z}_{i}=Z_{i}-\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[Z_{i}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})}}\right]$ , so that

$$ \displaystyle\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}} \displaystyle=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{Z}_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[Z_{i}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})}}\right]}}\right\|_{\textup{op}} \displaystyle\leqslant\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{Z}_{i}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[Z_{i}\mathds{1}(\|Z_{i}\|\leqslant d^{-t+\delta})}}\right]}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}\leqslant d^{\varepsilon/2}\Phi+CNd^{-k_{2}}\leqslant d^{\varepsilon}\Phi. $$

This shows that

$$ \mathbb{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}}}\right\|_{\textup{op}}>d^{\varepsilon}\Phi}}\right)\leqslant\mathbb{P}(\tilde{\Omega}(N,\varepsilon,D)^{c})\leqslant N^{-D}, $$

which finishes the proof. ∎

## 6 Basic tools: Preliminary bounds

The goal of this section is to prove several preliminary bounds on various quantities that we will use later. All of the estimates used outside of this section are summarized in the statements of Lemmas 6.2 and 6.3.

#### Lemma 6.1.

Let $B_{j}$ be the $j$ th column of $B$ with the $(j,j)$ th entry (which is zero) removed. Then

$$ \max_{j=1}^{N}\|B_{j}\|\prec 1. $$

#### Proof.

Since the distribution of $\|B_{j}\|$ does not depend on $j$ , it suffices to prove $\|B_{j}\|\prec 1$ . We also prefer to split

$$ (U^{\ast}TU)_{ij}=\sum_{\mu}U_{\mu i}T_{\mu}U_{\mu j}=\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\sum_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}U_{\mu i}T_{\mu}U_{\mu j}=\vcentcolon\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}V^{(k)}_{ij}, $$

which suggests that we decompose $B_{j}$ into a sum of vectors

$$ B_{j}=\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}V_{j}^{(k)}, $$

where $V_{j}^{(k)}$ is the vector whose $i$ th entry is $V_{ij}^{(k)}$ . Then

$$ \|B_{j}\|\leqslant\sum_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\|V_{j}^{(k)}\|. $$

Since this sum has a constant number of terms, it suffices to show that $\|V_{j}^{(k)}\|\prec 1$ for any $k\in\llbracket\lceil\ell\rceil,L\rrbracket$ . Now we compute high moments of $\|V_{j}^{(k)}\|$ . For $p\in\mathbb{N}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\|V_{j}^{(k)}\|^{2p}}}\right] \displaystyle=\sum_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{p}}^{(j)}\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{a=1}^{p}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(V_{i_{a}j}^{(k)}}}\right)^{2}}}\right] \displaystyle=T_{k}^{2p}\sum_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{p}}^{(j)}\sum_{\mu_{1},\nu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{p},\nu_{p}\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{a=1}^{p}U_{\mu_{a}i_{a}}U_{\nu_{a}i_{a}}}}\right]\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\prod_{a=1}^{p}U_{\mu_{a}j}U_{\nu_{a}j}}}\right] $$

where the last expectations factor since all the $i_{a}$ ’s are distinct from $j$ . The expectations vanish unless the $X$ ’s pair, so $\sum_{\mu_{1},\nu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{p}\nu_{p}\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}$ has order $d^{kp}$ nonzero terms instead of the naive $d^{2kp}$ ; each product of expectations contributes order $N^{-2p}$ ; we have $T_{k}^{2p}=C_{2p}N^{p}d^{-kp}$ , and $\sum_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{p}}^{(j)}$ contributes $N^{p}$ , so

$$ \mathbb{E}[\|V_{j}^{(k)}\|^{2p}]\leqslant C_{2p}, $$

which concludes the proof. ∎

#### Lemma 6.2.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\min_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{jj}(z)}}\right\rvert\succ 1, \displaystyle\min_{j=1}^{N}\im(G_{jj}(z))\succ 1, $$

and therefore

$$ \displaystyle 1\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)}}\right\rvert\prec 1, \displaystyle 1\prec\im(s(z))\prec 1. $$

#### Proof.

Since $G_{jj}$ is a diagonal element of the resolvent of $B$ , which has $B_{jj}=0$ , the Schur complement formula gives us

$$ G_{jj}=\frac{1}{-z-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},(B^{(j)}-z)^{-1}B_{j}}}\right\rangle} $$

where $B_{j}$ is the $j$ th column of $B$ except for the $(j,j)$ element, and $B^{(j)}$ is the corresponding minor. Since $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert z}}\right\rvert$ is order one, Lemma 6.1 gives

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},(B^{(j)}-z)^{-1}B_{j}}}\right\rangle}}\right\rvert\leqslant\|(B^{(j)}-z)^{-1}\|_{\textup{op}}\|B_{j}\|^{2}\leqslant\frac{1}{\eta}\|B_{j}\|^{2}\prec 1 $$

which proves (6.1). For (6.2), we note that, if $(u_{i})_{i=1}^{N-1}$ is a (real) orthonormal eigenbasis for $B^{(j)}$ with corresponding eigenvalues $(\lambda_{i})_{i=1}^{N-1}$ , then

$$ \im\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},(B^{(j)}-z)^{-1}B_{j}}}\right\rangle}}\right)=\im\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i}-z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},u_{i}}}\right\rangle^{2}}}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\frac{\eta}{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\lambda_{i}-z}}\right\rvert^{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},u_{i}}}\right\rangle^{2}\geqslant 0, $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\im G_{jj} \displaystyle=\frac{\im(\overline{-z-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},(B^{(j)}-z)^{-1}B_{j}}}\right\rangle})}{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert-z-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},(B^{(j)}-z)^{-1}B_{j}}}\right\rangle}}\right\rvert^{2}}=\frac{\im(z)+\im(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},(B^{(j)}-z)^{-1}B_{j}}}\right\rangle)}{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert-z-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},(B^{(j)}-z)^{-1}B_{j}}}\right\rangle}}\right\rvert^{2}} \displaystyle\geqslant\frac{\im(z)}{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert-z-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle B_{j},(B^{(j)}-z)^{-1}B_{j}}}\right\rangle}}\right\rvert^{2}}=\im(z)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{jj}}}\right\rvert^{2}. $$

Now we put a minimum over $j$ , apply (6.1), and use $\im(z)\succ 1$ to obtain (6.2).

The lower bound in (6.4) follows immediately from (6.2). On the event $\{\im(s(z))>0\}$ , we have $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)}}\right\rvert\geqslant\im(s(z))$ ; this implies $1\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)}}\right\rvert$ . Similarly, the upper bound in (6.4) follows from the upper bound in (6.3), which is immediate since $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert s(z)}}\right\rvert\leqslant\frac{1}{\eta}$ deterministically as the trace of a resolvent. ∎

#### Lemma 6.3.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\max_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\frac{d^{k}}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}(z)+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\prec 1, \displaystyle\max_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\max_{i=1}^{N}\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}d^{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}^{(i)}(z)-G_{M}(z))_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\prec 1, \displaystyle\max_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\max_{i=1}^{N}\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\frac{d^{k}}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G^{(i)}_{M}(z)+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert \displaystyle\prec 1. $$

In order to prove this lemma, we need the control parameters

$$ \displaystyle\Lambda_{c}(z) \displaystyle=\max_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\max_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\max_{j=1}^{N}\frac{d^{k/2}}{\sqrt{N}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|(G_{M}(z))_{\nu j}}}\right|, \displaystyle\Lambda_{d}(z) \displaystyle=\max_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\frac{d^{k}}{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}(z)+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert, $$

as well as the following two lemmas:

#### Lemma 6.4.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \max_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\max_{i=1}^{N}\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}d^{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}^{(i)}-G_{M})_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec N\Lambda_{c}(z)^{2}. $$

#### Lemma 6.5.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ and any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\Lambda_{c}(z)\prec\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda_{d}(z)+\Lambda_{c}(z)^{2}+1}{N}}, \displaystyle\Lambda_{d}(z)\prec\sqrt{\Lambda_{d}(z)+\Lambda_{c}(z)^{2}+1}. $$

From here the proof is straightforward:

#### Proof of Lemma 6.3, modulo Lemmas 6.4 and 6.5.

From the definition of stochastic domination, it is an elementary exercise to verify, for $X_{N}$ and $Y_{N}$ positive and real, that $X_{N}\prec\frac{X_{N}}{N}+Y_{N}$ implies $X_{N}\prec Y_{N}$ ; thus one upgrades (6.9) into

$$ \Lambda_{c}(z)\prec\sqrt{\frac{\Lambda_{d}(z)+1}{N}}. $$

Plugging this into (6.10), one obtains similarly

$$ \Lambda_{d}(z)\prec\sqrt{\Lambda_{d}(z)+\frac{\Lambda_{d}(z)+1}{N}+1}\prec\sqrt{\Lambda_{d}(z)+1}, $$

from which it is another elementary exercise from the definition of stochastic domination to conclude $\Lambda_{d}(z)\prec 1$ , which is exactly (6.5). Plugging this back into (6.11), one obtains

$$ \Lambda_{c}(z)\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}. $$

Combining this with Lemma 6.4 yields (6.6). Finally, (6.7) is immediate from combining (6.5) and (6.6). ∎

The proofs of Lemmas 6.4 and 6.5 regularly use the following short lemma. The proof is a short exercise in the definition of stochastic domination, so we omit it.

#### Lemma 6.6.

Suppose we have random variables $X_{N,k,i,\mu}$ depending on $k\in\llbracket\lceil\ell\rceil,L\rrbracket$ , on $i\in\llbracket 1,N\rrbracket$ , and on $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}$ , such that for some $Y_{N}$ we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert X_{N,k,i,\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec Y_{N} $$

for each $k$ , $i$ , and $\mu$ . If, for each fixed $k$ , the distribution of $X_{N,k,i,\mu}$ depends neither on $i$ nor on $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}$ , then

$$ \max_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\max_{i=1}^{N}\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert X_{N,k,i,\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec Y_{N}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 6.4.

Combining the resolvent identity $G^{(i)}_{\mu\mu}=G_{\mu\mu}-\frac{G_{\mu i}G_{i\mu}}{G_{ii}}$ from (4.1) with $\min_{j=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{jj}(z)}}\right\rvert\succ 1$ from (6.1), we obtain

$$ d^{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}^{(i)}-G_{M})_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec N\Lambda_{c}(z)^{2} $$

for each $k$ , $i$ , and $\mu$ . Applying Lemma 6.6 completes the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 6.5.

First, we claim that for each $\mu$ and each $i$ we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}U_{\nu i}G^{(i)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sqrt{\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G^{(i)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert^{2}}. $$

Indeed, by summing over $k\in\llbracket\lceil\ell\rceil,L\rrbracket$ , to show (6.12) it suffices to show

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}U_{\nu i}G^{(i)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sqrt{\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G^{(i)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert^{2}} $$

for each $k$ ; we write this in terms of the $X$ ’s, cancelling the factor $1/\sqrt{N}$ , as

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{a_{1}<\cdots<a_{k}}^{d}X_{a_{1}i}\cdots X_{a_{k}i}G^{(i)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\sqrt{\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G^{(i)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert^{2}}, $$

where $\nu=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})$ . But estimates of this form are essentially standard, and are typically called “large deviations bounds” in the local-law literature. Simple ones take the form $\sum_{a_{1}\neq a_{2}}X_{a_{1}}X_{a_{2}}b_{a_{1}a_{2}}\prec(\sum_{a_{1}\neq a_{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert b_{a_{1}a_{2}}}}\right\rvert^{2})^{1/2}$ (see, e.g., [EKYY13b, Theorem C.1], which is based on [EKYY13a, Lemmas B.2–B.4]), where the $X_{a}$ ’s are i.i.d. centered random variables with unit variance, the $b_{a_{1}a_{2}}$ are deterministic, and the result is crucially uniform in $b_{a_{1}a_{2}}$ . In our case, the sum is over $k$ indices rather than two, but this generalization is routine, as already noted in [EKYY13b, Theorem C.1] and [EKYY13a, Lemmas B.2–B.4]. Furthermore, in our case the role of $b_{a_{1}a_{2}}$ is played instead by $G^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}$ . These resolvent entries are not deterministic, but they are independent of $X_{i}$ , so we can condition on them; since the result is uniform in deterministic $b_{a_{1}a_{2}}$ , we can safely integrate over the randomness in $G^{(i)}$ , obtaining (6.13) and thus (6.12).

Now fix $k$ and $\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}$ . On the one hand, if we start with the resolvent identity $G_{i\mu}=-G_{ii}\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}U_{\nu i}G_{\nu\mu}^{(i)}$ from (4.2) and use the estimates $\max_{i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{ii}}}\right\rvert\leqslant 1/\eta\prec 1$ , which is trivial since the $G_{ii}$ are the diagonal elements of a resolvent, and (6.12), we obtain

$$ \max_{i=1}^{N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{i\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\max_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sqrt{\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{\nu\mu}^{(i)}}}\right\rvert^{2}}. $$

On the other hand, if we start with the resolvent identity $(G_{M}+T)_{\mu\mu}=-T_{\mu}\sum_{i=1}^{N}G_{ii}\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}U_{\mu i}U_{\nu i}G_{\nu\mu}^{(i)}$ , from (4.5), and use $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert U_{\mu j}}}\right\rvert\prec 1/\sqrt{N}$ as well as (6.12) (to which we can add $\max_{i=1}^{N}$ on both sides by Lemma 6.6), we obtain

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}+T)_{\mu\mu}}}\right\rvert\prec\sqrt{\frac{N}{d^{k}}}\max_{i=1}^{N}\sqrt{\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G^{(i)}_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert^{2}}. $$

Assume momentarily the estimate

$$ \frac{d^{k}}{N}\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{\nu\mu}^{(i)}}}\right\rvert^{2}\prec\Lambda_{e}(z)+\Lambda_{c}(z)^{2}+1. $$

Lemma 6.6 allows us to add $\max_{k=\lceil\ell\rceil}^{L}\max_{i=1}^{N}\max_{\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k}}$ to the left-hand side for free. Combining this with (6.14) yields (6.9); combining it with (6.15) instead yields (6.10).

Thus it remains only to prove (6.16). We do this using the full Ward inequality, Lemma 5.1: Since $T$ is diagonal and $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert a+b}}\right\rvert^{2}\leqslant 2\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert a}}\right\rvert^{2}+2\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert b}}\right\rvert^{2}\prec\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert a}}\right\rvert^{2}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert b}}\right\rvert^{2}$ , we find

$$ \sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{\nu\mu}^{(i)}}}\right\rvert^{2}=\sum_{\nu}^{(\mu)}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}^{(i)}+T)_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert^{2}+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G_{M}^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\mu}-T_{\mu}}}\right\rvert^{2}\prec\sum_{\nu\in\mathbf{M}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert(G^{(i)}+T)_{\nu\mu}}}\right\rvert^{2}+T_{\mu}^{2}\prec\frac{\im G_{\mu\mu}^{(i)}}{\eta}+\frac{N}{d^{k}}. $$

Since $T$ is real, we have

$$ \frac{\im G_{\mu\mu}^{(i)}}{\eta}\prec\im G_{\mu\mu}^{(i)}=\im(G_{M}^{(i)}-G_{M})_{\mu\mu}+\im(G_{M}+T)_{\mu\mu}\prec\frac{N}{d^{k}}(\Lambda_{e}(z)+\Lambda_{c}(z)^{2}), $$

which completes the proof of (6.16), and thus of the lemma. ∎

## 7 Self-consistent equations I: Proof of Proposition 3.2

In this section, we prove Proposition 3.2. The bulk of the proof is Lemma 7.1, which says roughly that, for each $i$ , we have $\sum_{\mu,\nu}U_{\mu i}(G^{(i)}_{M}+T)_{\mu\nu}U_{\nu i}\approx\phi\widetilde{s}$ . This should be thought of as a kind of concentration result: Since $\mathbb{E}[U_{\mu i}U_{\nu i}]=\delta_{\mu\nu}/N$ and $G_{M}^{(i)}+T$ is independent of the $X_{i}$ ’s, the partial expectation of $\sum_{\mu,\nu}U_{\mu i}(G^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\nu}U_{\nu i}$ over just the $X_{i}$ ’s is $\frac{1}{N}\Tr(G^{(i)}_{M}+T)$ ; and if one replaces $G^{(i)}_{M}$ with $G_{M}$ in this expression, one gets exactly $\phi\widetilde{s}$ . Lemma 7.1 itself relies fundamentally on the partial Ward inequalities from Section 5.

#### Lemma 7.1.

For any fixed $\tau>0$ , any fixed $z\in\mathbf{D}_{\tau}$ , and any $i\in[N]$ , we have

$$ \mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert\sum_{\mu,\nu}U_{\mu i}(G_{M}^{(i)}(z)+T)_{\mu\nu}U_{\nu i}-\phi\widetilde{s}(z)}}\right\rvert\prec\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 3.2, modulo Lemma 7.1.

From the Schur complement formula (4.3) and Lemma 7.1, we have

$$ \displaystyle G_{ii}^{-1} \displaystyle=-z-\sum_{\mu,\nu}U_{\mu i}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(G_{M}^{(i)}+T}}\right)_{\mu\nu}U_{\nu i}=-z-\phi\tilde{s}(z)+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}}}\right). $$

Multiplying both sides by $G_{ii}$ and using the deterministic bound $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{ii}}}\right\rvert\leqslant 1/\eta$ (so that $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lvert G_{ii}}}\right\rvert\OO_{\prec}(d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)})=\OO_{\prec}(d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)})$ ), we find

$$ 1=(-z-\phi\widetilde{s}(z))G_{ii}+\OO_{\prec}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{d^{\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}}}}\right). $$

The error term is uniform in $i$ , since all the variables are exchangeable in $i$ . Thus we can average both sides over $i$ and rearrange to obtain the result. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 7.1.

Since $\phi\widetilde{s}=\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{tr}(G_{M}+T)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu}(G_{M}+T)_{\mu\mu}$ , it suffices to show the following three bounds:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{1} \displaystyle\vcentcolon=\sum_{\mu\neq\nu}U_{\mu i}(G^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\nu}U_{\nu i}=\sum_{\mu\neq\nu}U_{\mu i}G^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}U_{\nu i}\prec d^{-\frac{1}{2}\min(1,\ell)}, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{2} \displaystyle\vcentcolon=\sum_{\mu}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(U_{\mu i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N}}}\right)(G^{(i)}+T)_{\mu\mu}\prec\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}, \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{3} \displaystyle\vcentcolon=\frac{1}{N}(\mathrm{tr}(G^{(i)}_{M})-\mathrm{tr}(G_{M}))\prec\frac{1}{d^{\ell}}. $$

Notice that the $\min$ only appears in the estimate of $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ , and that the estimate on $\mathcal{E}_{3}$ is much better than needed. First we consider the $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ term, which is the most complicated. It is convenient to split the sum over all $\mu\neq\nu$ into terms which fix the length of (number of $X$ ’s contained in) $\mu$ , fix the length of $\nu$ , and fix their overlap, by defining

$$ \mathcal{G}^{(k_{1},k_{2},s)}\vcentcolon=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle(\mu,\nu):\mu\neq\nu,\mu\in\mathbf{M}_{k_{1}},\nu\in\mathbf{M}_{k_{2}},\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle\mu,\nu}}\right\rangle=s}}\right\rangle $$

and

$$ \mathcal{E}_{1,k_{1},k_{2},s}\vcentcolon=\sum_{(\mu,\nu)\in\mathcal{G}^{(k_{1},k_{2},s)}}U_{\mu i}G^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}U_{\nu i}=\frac{\alpha_{k_{1},k_{2},s}}{N}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a_{1},\ldots,a_{k_{1}}\\
b_{s+1},\ldots,b_{k_{2}}\end{subarray}}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{1}i}^{2}\ldots X_{a_{s}i}^{2}\cdot X_{a_{s+1}i}\ldots X_{a_{k_{1}}i}G^{(i)}_{\mu\nu}X_{b_{s+1}i}\ldots X_{b_{k_{2}}i}, $$

where $\alpha_{k_{1},k_{2},s}=\frac{1}{s!(k_{1}-s)!(k_{2}-s)!}$ is a combinatorial factor accounting for the fact that the indices in $\mu$ and $\nu$ are not only distinct but also ordered: We can reconstruct $\mu$ and $\nu$ from $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k_{1}})$ and $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{s},b_{s+1},\ldots,b_{k_{2}})$ just by ordering, but given $\mu$ and $\nu$ with $s$ shared indices, there are $s!$ ways to label the shared indices as $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{s})$ , $(k_{1}-s)!$ ways to label the remaining $\mu$ indices as $(a_{s+1},\ldots,a_{k_{1}})$ , and $(k_{2}-s)!$ ways to label the remaining $\nu$ indices as $(b_{s+1},\ldots,b_{k_{2}})$ . Thus $\alpha_{k_{1},k_{2},s}\prec 1$ , which is shortly how we will absorb it.

For fixed $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ , the possible $s$ values range from $0$ up to $\min(k_{1},k_{2})$ , unless $k_{1}=k_{2}=k$ , in which case the range is $s\in\llbracket 0,k-1\rrbracket$ , since if $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\langle\mu,\nu}}\right\rangle$ equals the common length of $\mu$ and $\nu$ , then $\mu=\nu$ , which is forbidden in the sum.

Notice $\mathcal{E}_{1}=\sum_{k_{1},k_{2},s}\mathcal{E}_{1,k_{1},k_{2},s}$ ; since $(k_{1},k_{2},s)$ takes values in a finite set, we can estimate each $\mathcal{E}_{1,k_{1},k_{2},s}$ separately. Now for each $\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}\}$ all distinct we write

$$ S_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}}=\sum_{a_{s+1},\ldots,a_{k_{1}},b_{s+1},\ldots,b_{k_{2}}=1}^{d,\ast}X_{a_{s+1}i}\cdots X_{a_{k_{1}}i}G_{\mu\nu}^{(i)}X_{b_{s+1}i}\cdots X_{b_{k_{2}}i}, $$

where for each $a_{s+1},\ldots,a_{k_{1}},b_{s+1},\ldots,b_{k_{2}}$ , the $\mu$ and $\nu$ inside the sum denote the (reordered as necessary) tuples $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k_{1}})$ and $(a_{1},\ldots,a_{s},b_{s+1},\ldots,b_{k_{2}})$ , respectively.
